title: SAXON Q and Fraunhofer IWU Demonstrate Record 3-Qubit Grover Search on Commercial Room-Temperature Quantum Computer - Quantum Computing Report
gist: SAXON Q and Fraunhofer IWU ran a 3-qubit Grover search on a commercial room-temperature NV-center diamond quantum computer, reporting 77.3% and 87.0% success rates that beat prior room-temperature searches and rival cryogenic superconducting results. The machine draws about 600 W with no cryostat.

insights.claim: A commercial nitrogen-vacancy diamond quantum computer at Fraunhofer IWU in Dresden ran a 3-qubit Grover search with an average success probability of 77.3% (+/-3.4%) for one marked state out of eight, versus a 37.5% classical maximum.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shows a non-cryogenic platform clearing the classical bound on a standard algorithm; watch for replication on larger search spaces.

insights.claim: With two marked states out of eight, the SAXON Q NV-center system reached an 87.0% (+/-4.2%) average success probability against a 46.4% classical maximum, close to the 89.4% silicon spin-qubit result obtained at 15 mK with post-selection.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Room-temperature results now sit near the best cryogenic spin figures, narrowing the performance gap that justified dilution refrigerators.

insights.claim: The reported success rates surpass previous room-temperature quantum searches and rival benchmarks set by cryogenic superconducting processors, which the article cites at 49.2%-78.0%, with trapped ions at 43.7%-69.0%.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Competitive small-scale algorithm fidelity is the claim to test as rivals publish like-for-like Grover runs.

insights.claim: The system operated at an average 296.3 K (23.1 C) and required no cryostats, optical traps, or vacuum chambers, drawing roughly 600 watts continuously.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Removing cryogenic infrastructure cuts siting, cooling, and operating cost, supporting on-premises deployment.
insights.quote: required no cryostats, optical traps, or vacuum chambers

insights.claim: Cryogenic superconducting systems the article uses as baselines rely on dilution refrigerators below 20 mK drawing 25+ kW, roughly 40 times the power of the room-temperature NV system.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Power and cooling overhead is a structural cost disadvantage for superconducting scale-up that room-temperature modalities could exploit.

insights.claim: The computing register uses solid-state nuclear spins, namely the intrinsic nitrogen-14 nucleus and two nearby carbon-13 nuclei, with the NV electronic spin serving only as an optical interface for initialization, entangling operations, and readout.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Separating memory (nuclear) from interface (electronic) spin is the design lever behind the long coherence reported.

insights.claim: Nuclear spin qubits shielded by the carbon lattice show T2 coherence of 1.4 to 4.3 milliseconds, roughly 1,000 times longer than the NV center's electronic spin.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Long coherence is what makes multi-gate algorithms feasible at ambient temperature.

insights.claim: Single-qubit gate fidelity averaged 99.90% Clifford (up to 99.98%) by randomized benchmarking, and multi-qubit subspace fidelity averaged 95.7% for the Phase000 gate via interleaved RB.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Two-qubit-class fidelity near 95.7% is the weaker figure and the limiter to scaling beyond three qubits.

insights.claim: SAXON Q already offers commercially a 128-qubit SXQ128 and a 512-qubit SXQ512 modular multi-core system, and this Grover demonstration is presented as complementing that hardware roadmap.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The gap between a 3-qubit algorithm demo and the claimed 128/512-qubit products is worth scrutinizing for evidence of algorithm-level performance at scale.
